title: A full stack with Docker Compose
intro: Running a database, Spring Boot API, and React frontend as separate containers is useful, but starting and configuring them individually quickly becomes tedious. Docker Compose lets you describe the whole application stack in one file, including services, networks, persistent volumes, environment variables, dependencies, and health checks.
body:
## Why Docker Compose matters

In the previous lesson, you learned how to build and run individual Docker images. That is enough for a single application, but a real full-stack application usually contains several services.

Our mini webshop has three main parts:

~~~text
React + nginx
     |
     v
Spring Boot API
     |
     v
PostgreSQL
~~~

You could start each container manually with several `docker run` commands. You would also need to create a network, configure environment variables, create persistent storage, and make sure the API does not try to use PostgreSQL before PostgreSQL is ready.

Docker Compose solves this coordination problem. You describe the desired stack declaratively in a `compose.yaml` file, then Docker Compose creates and starts the required resources for you.

A typical workflow becomes:

~~~text
docker compose up -d
        |
        v
   full stack running
        |
        v
docker compose logs -f
        |
        v
docker compose down
~~~

Compose is especially useful during local development, integration testing, and small deployments where several containers belong to one application.

---

## The compose.yaml file

Docker Compose normally uses a file named `compose.yaml` in the project directory.

A simplified file might look like this:

~~~yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16

  api:
    build: ./backend

  web:
    build: ./frontend
~~~

The `services` section defines the containers that make up the application.

Each service has a name. In this example, the names are `db`, `api`, and `web`.

The service name is important because Docker Compose creates a network for the application and makes service names available as hostnames inside that network.

For example, the Spring Boot application should not connect to PostgreSQL using `localhost`:

~~~text
jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/shop
~~~

Inside the `api` container, `localhost` means the API container itself. PostgreSQL is a different container.

Instead, the API connects to the `db` service:

~~~text
jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop
~~~

This is one of the most important ideas in Docker Compose: **service names become network hostnames**.

---

## Networks and service discovery

Compose automatically creates a network for the services in a project unless you configure networking differently.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "One network, three services", "caption": "Inside the Compose network, services find each other by name. Only published ports are reachable from your laptop.", "nodes": [{"id": "you", "label": "Your browser", "kind": "user"}, {"id": "web", "label": "web", "sub": "nginx · ports 80:80", "kind": "client", "highlight": true}, {"id": "api", "label": "api", "sub": "Spring Boot · 8080:8080", "kind": "server", "highlight": true}, {"id": "db", "label": "db", "sub": "postgres:16 · volume db-data", "kind": "db"}], "edges": [{"from": "you", "to": "web", "label": "localhost:80"}, {"from": "web", "to": "api", "label": "http://api:8080"}, {"from": "api", "to": "db", "label": "jdbc:postgresql://db:5432"}]}
~~~

Suppose the stack contains:

~~~yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16

  api:
    build: ./backend

  web:
    build: ./frontend
~~~

The containers can communicate using names such as:

~~~text
db
api
web
~~~

The API can reach PostgreSQL at `db:5432`. The frontend can reach another service at its service name when the communication happens from inside a container.

There is an important distinction for browser applications. JavaScript running in the user's browser is not running inside the Compose network. A browser cannot normally use `http://api:8080` because `api` is a Docker network hostname, not a hostname known to the user's computer.

For browser-to-API traffic, you usually expose the API through a host port or put a reverse proxy in front of the services.

---

## Building the PostgreSQL service

For the webshop database, we can define PostgreSQL like this:

~~~yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
      POSTGRES_USER: shop
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
~~~

The official PostgreSQL image reads these environment variables during initialization.

`POSTGRES_DB` specifies the initial database, while `POSTGRES_USER` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` define the initial database user.

For a real application, do not commit production passwords such as this example into source control. The example uses a simple password because it is easier to understand in a local learning environment.

Environment-specific configuration should be separated from the Compose definition when appropriate.

---

## Named volumes and persistent data

Containers are disposable. If you remove a PostgreSQL container without persistent storage, its database data can disappear with it.

A **named volume** provides storage managed by Docker that exists independently from the lifecycle of an individual container.

Add a volume to the database service:

~~~yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data:
~~~

The first `db-data` is the Docker volume name. The second path is where PostgreSQL stores its data inside the container.

The top-level `volumes` section declares the named volume.

This means you can remove and recreate the PostgreSQL container without automatically losing the database contents.

There is a useful distinction between:

~~~text
container lifecycle -> disposable
named volume       -> persistent
~~~

When you explicitly run `docker compose down -v`, however, Compose removes the named volumes associated with the stack. That is useful when you deliberately want a completely clean local environment, but it also means the database data is deleted.

---

## Health checks

Starting a PostgreSQL container does not necessarily mean PostgreSQL is ready to accept connections.

A container can be running while the application inside it is still initializing.

Docker Compose supports **health checks** to represent whether a service is actually ready.

For PostgreSQL, a useful health check is:

~~~yaml
healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shop"]
  interval: 5s
  retries: 5
~~~

`pg_isready` asks PostgreSQL whether it is accepting connections.

The `interval` controls how often Docker performs the check. `retries` controls how many unsuccessful checks are allowed before the service is considered unhealthy.

Health checks are especially useful when one service depends on another.

---

## depends_on and startup order

Compose also lets you describe dependencies between services.

~~~diagram
{"type": "sequence", "title": "Startup order with health checks", "actors": ["Compose", "db", "api", "web"], "steps": [{"from": "Compose", "to": "db", "label": "start"}, {"note": "pg_isready … healthy after ~5 s", "over": "db"}, {"from": "db", "to": "Compose", "label": "service_healthy", "dashed": true}, {"from": "Compose", "to": "api", "label": "start (depends_on: db healthy)"}, {"from": "api", "to": "db", "label": "Flyway migrate"}, {"from": "Compose", "to": "web", "label": "start"}]}
~~~

For example:

~~~yaml
api:
  build: ./backend
  depends_on:
    db:
      condition: service_healthy
~~~

This says that the API depends on the database being healthy before Compose starts the API according to this dependency condition.

Compare this with:

~~~yaml
web:
  build: ./frontend
  depends_on:
    api:
      condition: service_started
~~~

Here the frontend waits for the API service to be started, but it does not mean that every API endpoint is necessarily ready to process requests.

The distinction matters:

~~~text
service_started  -> the dependency has started
service_healthy  -> the dependency has passed its health check
~~~

For a database, `service_healthy` is usually much more useful than merely knowing that the container process started.

Application-level readiness can also be useful. A Spring Boot application can expose health information through Spring Boot Actuator. A Compose health check can then query an actuator health endpoint, for example through a command that checks whether the application responds successfully.

The exact command depends on what tools are available in the runtime image. A minimal JRE image may not contain `curl`, `wget`, or other HTTP clients, so health-check design needs to account for the actual image contents.

---

## The complete mini webshop stack

A small React + Spring Boot + PostgreSQL webshop can be represented like this:

~~~yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
      POSTGRES_USER: shop
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shop"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

  api:
    build: ./backend
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: shop
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: secret
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  web:
    build: ./frontend
    depends_on:
      api:
        condition: service_started
    ports:
      - "80:80"

volumes:
  db-data:
~~~

This file connects the three pieces together.

The database uses the official PostgreSQL image. The API is built from the `backend` directory. The frontend is built from the `frontend` directory.

The API uses `db` as the PostgreSQL hostname because `db` is the Compose service name.

The API publishes port 8080, while nginx publishes port 80. The database does not need a `ports` mapping for the API to connect to it because the services can communicate directly over the Compose network.

---

## ports versus expose

This distinction is easy to misunderstand.

`ports` publishes a container port to the host:

~~~yaml
ports:
  - "8080:8080"
~~~

This allows something outside the Compose network, such as your browser, to connect through the host's port 8080.

`expose` documents a port intended for communication between containers without publishing it to the host:

~~~yaml
expose:
  - "8080"
~~~

For many Compose configurations, containers can communicate over the internal network without needing `expose` at all. The service name and the application's listening port are what matter.

A good rule of thumb is:

~~~text
Browser -> API from host:     ports
API -> database internally:   internal Compose network
~~~

You generally should not publish a database port just because another container needs it.

---

## Environment files

Putting every configuration value directly into `compose.yaml` can become inconvenient, especially when different developers or environments need different values.

Compose supports environment files. A common local setup might use:

~~~text
.env
~~~

For example:

~~~text
POSTGRES_DB=shop
POSTGRES_USER=shop
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev
~~~

Compose can use variables from an environment file in the YAML configuration.

You should distinguish ordinary configuration from secrets. A `.env` file containing credentials should normally not be committed to Git. Add appropriate local secret files to `.gitignore` and provide production secrets through a suitable secret-management mechanism.

Environment files are a configuration convenience; they are not automatically a complete secrets-management solution.

---

## Starting the stack

Once your `compose.yaml` is ready, start the stack with:

~~~terms
[{"term": "docker compose up -d", "def": "Build if needed and start everything in the background."}, {"term": "docker compose logs -f api", "def": "Follow one service's log."}, {"term": "docker compose ps", "def": "Status and health of each service."}, {"term": "docker compose down -v", "def": "Stop and remove containers **and volumes** — your database data is gone."}]
~~~

~~~text
docker compose up -d
~~~

The `-d` option starts the containers in detached mode so your terminal remains available.

Compose creates the network, creates the named volume if necessary, builds images when required, and starts the services according to their dependencies.

To watch the logs:

~~~text
docker compose logs -f
~~~

The `-f` option follows the logs, similar to `tail -f`.

You can also focus on one service:

~~~text
docker compose logs -f api
~~~

This is particularly useful when debugging Spring Boot startup problems.

To stop and remove the containers and network created for the project:

~~~text
docker compose down
~~~

The named volume normally remains.

To remove the volumes as well:

~~~text
docker compose down -v
~~~

Use `-v` carefully. In the webshop example, it removes the PostgreSQL volume and therefore destroys the local database data stored there.

---

## A typical development workflow

Imagine you have this project structure:

~~~text
shop/
├── compose.yaml
├── backend/
│   ├── Dockerfile
│   ├── pom.xml
│   └── src/
└── frontend/
    ├── Dockerfile
    ├── package.json
    └── src/
~~~

From the `shop` directory, you can run:

~~~text
docker compose up -d
~~~

Then inspect the services:

~~~text
docker compose ps
~~~

Follow the API logs:

~~~text
docker compose logs -f api
~~~

Open the frontend in your browser and interact with the webshop.

If you need to stop the environment:

~~~text
docker compose down
~~~

The next `docker compose up -d` can recreate the containers while keeping the named database volume.

If you intentionally want to reset the local database completely:

~~~text
docker compose down -v
docker compose up -d
~~~

That gives you a clean PostgreSQL volume.

---

## Spring Boot health checks

Health checks become particularly valuable as the stack grows.

Spring Boot Actuator can expose application health information. A typical endpoint is:

~~~text
/actuator/health
~~~

A production-oriented application can expose this endpoint internally and use it as a readiness signal.

For example, conceptually a Compose health check could verify an HTTP endpoint:

~~~yaml
healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD-SHELL", "some-http-check http://localhost:8080/actuator/health"]
  interval: 10s
  retries: 5
~~~

The exact command depends on the runtime image. If your final image does not include an HTTP client, you can either add an appropriate tool deliberately or choose another health-check strategy.

The key idea is more important than the exact command: **health should represent application readiness, not merely process existence**.

This becomes increasingly important when services start at different speeds or recover after failures.

---

## Running Compose from IntelliJ IDEA

IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition is useful for working with the source files, Dockerfiles, and Compose configuration alongside the rest of your project.

With Docker integration available in your IntelliJ installation, Docker Compose configurations can be run from the IDE. The **Services** tool window provides a visual way to inspect containers, their status, logs, and related resources.

This can be convenient when developing locally because you can switch between code and running services without constantly changing terminal windows.

However, the CLI remains important. CI servers and remote Linux machines may not have IntelliJ installed, so commands such as:

~~~text
docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f
docker compose down
~~~

should be familiar to you.

Think of IntelliJ's integration as a convenience layer over the same Docker concepts rather than a replacement for understanding them.

---

## Common mistakes

### Using localhost between containers

`localhost` inside the API container refers to the API container. Use the Compose service name, such as `db`, when connecting to PostgreSQL from the API.

### Publishing every port

Not every service needs to be reachable from the host. The API may need a published port for local browser requests, but PostgreSQL can remain internal to the Compose network.

### Assuming depends_on means ready

A started container is not necessarily a ready application. Use health checks and appropriate dependency conditions where readiness matters.

### Accidentally deleting the database

`docker compose down -v` removes named volumes. Use it when you intentionally want to reset local persistent data, not as your default shutdown command.

### Committing credentials

A Compose file or `.env` file containing real passwords should not be casually committed to source control. Separate configuration from secrets and use appropriate secret handling for production.

### Making health checks depend on unavailable tools

A minimal runtime image may not contain `curl`, `wget`, or other utilities. Always verify that the command used by a health check exists inside the target image.

### Confusing browser networking with Docker networking

A browser running on your laptop is outside the Compose network. Docker service names such as `api` work between containers, not automatically from browser JavaScript.

---

## What Compose gives you

Docker Compose is valuable because it turns a collection of manually configured containers into a reproducible application environment.

For the webshop, one Compose file describes:

- PostgreSQL and its initial configuration.
- Persistent database storage.
- A PostgreSQL readiness check.
- The Spring Boot API and its database connection.
- The API's dependency on a healthy database.
- The React/nginx frontend.
- The frontend's dependency on the API starting.
- Host ports for the services that need external access.
- The internal network through which services discover one another.

That is a substantial amount of infrastructure represented by one declarative configuration file.

The next step toward real DevOps is to automate this process. Instead of manually building images and starting Compose, a CI/CD pipeline can test the application, build the images, publish them, and deploy a known version to a server.

Docker packages the application. Compose coordinates the local multi-container application. CI/CD will eventually automate the journey from a Git commit to a running deployment.
takeaways: Docker Compose describes a multi-container application through services, networks, volumes, configuration, and dependencies.
Compose service names such as db become hostnames on the internal application network.
Named volumes keep database data separate from the disposable database container.
Health checks and service_healthy dependencies let services wait for actual readiness instead of only container startup.
ports publishes container ports to the host, while internal service communication normally uses the Compose network.
docker compose up, logs, and down provide the basic lifecycle workflow for a local full-stack environment.

quiz.question: Why should the Spring Boot API use `db` instead of `localhost` in its PostgreSQL JDBC URL?
options: Because PostgreSQL only supports the hostname `db`
Because `db` is the Compose service name and can be resolved inside the Compose network
Because localhost is disabled by Docker
Because the API cannot use TCP connections to PostgreSQL
quiz.explanation: Compose services can discover one another by service name on the internal network. Inside the API container, localhost refers to the API container itself, not the PostgreSQL container.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a named volume for PostgreSQL?
options: To publish PostgreSQL to the internet
To make PostgreSQL run faster
To keep database data independent from the lifecycle of the container
To automatically create database users
quiz.explanation: A named volume stores database data outside the disposable container filesystem, allowing the container to be recreated while retaining the data.

quiz.question: What does `condition: service_healthy` mean in a `depends_on` configuration?
options: The dependency must pass its configured health check before the dependent service starts according to that condition
The dependency must expose every container port
The dependency must use PostgreSQL
The dependency can never be restarted
quiz.explanation: service_healthy uses the dependency's health status rather than merely checking whether its container process has started.

quiz.question: What happens when you run `docker compose down -v`?
options: It rebuilds every image
It only follows the logs
It publishes all service ports
It removes the Compose resources and associated named volumes
quiz.explanation: The `-v` option tells Compose to remove named volumes associated with the project. For a PostgreSQL service, this can delete local database data.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes `ports` in a Compose service?
options: It creates a named Docker volume
It maps a host port to a container port
It makes the service healthy
It defines the service's database schema
quiz.explanation: A mapping such as `8080:8080` publishes the container's port 8080 through port 8080 on the host.

exercise.title: Build a Compose stack and resolve service dependencies
exercise.task:
Define exactly these two functions:

1. `function composeFile()` — return a plain object with this structure and these exact values:
   - `services.db.image` must be `"postgres:16"`.
   - `services.db.environment` must contain `POSTGRES_DB: "shop"`, `POSTGRES_USER: "shop"`, and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "secret"`.
   - `services.db.volumes` must contain `"db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"`.
   - `services.db.healthcheck.test` must be `["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U shop"]`.
   - `services.db.healthcheck.interval` must be `"5s"` and `retries` must be `5`.
   - `services.api.build` must be `"./backend"`.
   - `services.api.environment` must contain the PostgreSQL JDBC URL using host `db`, plus the username and password shown in the requested structure.
   - `services.api.depends_on.db.condition` must be `"service_healthy"`.
   - `services.api.ports` must contain `"8080:8080"`.
   - `services.web.build` must be `"./frontend"`.
   - `services.web.depends_on.api.condition` must be `"service_started"`.
   - `services.web.ports` must contain `"80:80"`.
   - The top-level `volumes` object must declare `"db-data"` as an empty object.

2. `function startOrder(services)` — take an object like `composeFile().services`. `depends_on` may be an array of service names, an object keyed by service names, or missing. Return the service names in an order where every service appears after all of its dependencies. When multiple services are ready at the same time, choose them in alphabetical order. Throw an `Error` whose message contains `"cycle"` when the dependency graph contains a cycle. Throw an `Error` whose message contains `"unknown"` when a service depends on a service that does not exist.

Do not mutate the input object passed to `startOrder`.
exercise.hint: For `composeFile`, construct the nested object directly and make sure the API JDBC URL uses the service name `db`, not `localhost`. For `startOrder`, first normalize each `depends_on` value into an array of dependency names. Validate that every dependency exists, then repeatedly select services with no remaining dependencies in alphabetical order. Remove the selected services from the remaining dependency sets. If no service is ready while services remain, the graph contains a cycle. Work with copied arrays, Sets, and maps so the original input is never modified.

tests.name: It defines the PostgreSQL service correctly
It uses the db service name in the JDBC URL
It configures the PostgreSQL healthcheck
tests.code:
const healthcheck = composeFile()?.services?.db?.healthcheck;
return Array.isArray(healthcheck?.test) &&
  healthcheck.test.length === 2 &&
  healthcheck.test[0] === "CMD-SHELL" &&
  healthcheck.test[1] === "pg_isready -U shop" &&
  healthcheck.interval === "5s" &&
  healthcheck.retries === 5;

tests.name: It declares the named database volume
It orders the Compose stack as db, api, web
It supports array dependencies
It uses alphabetical order for services ready at the same time
It throws an error containing cycle for cyclic dependencies
It throws an error containing unknown for a missing dependency and does not mutate input
